analysis.one_liner: Replaces the income and estate taxes with a 15% national sales tax and shuts down the IRS.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Tauzin with 3 cosponsors, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on April 2, 2004, and died there without a hearing or vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the federal income tax, the estate and gift taxes, and several excise taxes effective July 2006, replacing them with a 15% national sales tax on goods and services [S2, S3]. It would phase out the IRS after 2007, let states collect the tax for a 1% fee, and require a two-thirds vote of either chamber to raise the sales tax rate or pass any bill that cuts federal revenue [S2, S3]. Low-wage families would get a rebate covering the tax up to the poverty level, paid through paychecks [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: The largest winners would be high-income households, whose taxes on wages, capital gains, and inherited wealth would disappear, leaving them taxed only on what they spend [S2, S3]. Businesses would no longer pay income taxes and would get credits for compliance costs and administrative work [S3]. Low-wage working families would get a rebate covering the sales tax on spending up to the poverty level, and tuition for education and job training would be exempt [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal income tax, the estate and gift taxes, and certain excise taxes effective for taxable years beginning after June 30, 2006 [S2, S3].
Exempts business purchases, exports, and education tuition from the sales tax, and gives businesses an administrative credit and a credit for half the cost of new compliance equipment [S3].
Provides a monthly rebate through paychecks covering the sales tax on consumption up to the federal poverty level for each family unit, and compensating payments for people on fixed incomes [S2, S3].
Lets states that adopt a conforming sales tax collect the federal tax in exchange for a 1% administration fee [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who buys goods and services would pay the new 15% tax, which is levied on the gross payment including the tax itself, so the effective rate on a purchase is higher than 15% [S3]. Because lower- and middle-income households spend most of their income while wealthy households can save much of theirs, the tax falls proportionally hardest on ordinary consumers; the rebate offsets this only up to the poverty level [S3]. With income, estate, and certain excise taxes repealed, federal revenue would shift from wealth and earnings to consumption.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, especially low- and middle-income households

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to gross payments inclusive of the tax, so a listed 15% rate corresponds to a higher effective rate on the underlying price of a purchase [S3].
Wages paid by employers that are not registered active businesses, including government employers, would themselves be treated as taxable services, adding a tax layer to public-sector payrolls [S3].

Home purchases would owe the full sales tax, softened only by an option to pay it in equal installments over 30 years with interest, and unpaid installments come due within two years if the home is sold or stops being the buyer's principal residence [S3].

Repealing the income, estate, gift, and excise taxes while replacing them with a single 15% rate would not raise equivalent revenue at current federal spending levels, implying pressure for spending cuts or higher rates later [S2].

The bill would require a two-thirds vote in either chamber to raise the sales tax rate or to consider any legislation that reduces federal revenues, locking in the new structure beyond ordinary legislative rules [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a progressive income tax, which rises with earnings and wealth, for a consumption tax, which takes a larger share of income from households that must spend everything they earn. Its poverty-level rebate softens the hit to the lowest-wage families, and education and business purchases are exempt, but households earning modestly above the poverty line would pay the full tax on nearly all their spending while the tax burden on large estates, capital gains, and high incomes disappears. Even sympathetic analysts would flag the revenue gap: a 15% rate on the tax-inclusive base would not replace the revenue being repealed, so the design either underfunds the government or invites rate increases the bill's own supermajority rule is meant to block.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from its April 2004 referral until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S1, S5].

narrative.text: Rep. W. J. (Billy) Tauzin introduced the bill on April 2, 2004, with Reps. Burton, DeMint, and Norwood as the only cosponsors, all Republicans [S3, S4, S5].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation, and also to the Rules Committee [S1, S5].
No further action was recorded before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, so the bill expired without a vote [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing income tax structure stayed in place, so households whose taxes would have risen under the sales tax were spared, and industries built around the income tax, like tax preparation and estate planning, kept their business. No one gained the bill's intended benefits; high earners never got the repeal they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo held for everyone

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it never reached a recorded vote [S4, S5].

industries.note: The bill repeals the income tax, capital gains taxation, and the estate and gift taxes, so the wealthiest households would stop paying taxes on earnings and inheritances and pay only on consumption they choose [S2, S3]. Because the offsetting tax falls on consumption, which weighs heaviest on lower- and middle-income families, the gain for concentrated wealth comes largely at ordinary consumers' expense [S3].

industries.industry: Tax preparation, accounting, and estate planning services
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and defunding the IRS after 2007 would eliminate most of this industry's core business [S2, S3]. The industry's interest in the bill failing was aligned with keeping the tax system ordinary taxpayers already navigate, though the bill promised to reduce taxpayers' compliance burdens [S2].

Sellers would bear new registration, collection, and remittance duties with penalties, but would receive an administrative credit of up to 20% of tax due and a credit for half the cost of new compliance equipment [S3]. Whether the compensation outweighed the burden would vary by firm size and sales volume.

The bill would tax financial intermediation services, including brokerage fees, loan fees, insurance premiums, and an imputed tax on interest spreads [S3]. Their higher-income clients would benefit from the repeal of taxes on investment income, but the institutions themselves would take on a new tax and compliance regime [S3].
States that adopt a conforming sales tax could collect the federal tax for a 1% administration fee, a new revenue stream for state treasuries [S2, S3].

The bill imposes its 15% tax directly on gross gaming receipts minus payoffs, paid by the operator [S3]. Gaming operators' interest in avoiding the tax ran against the bill's stated goal of taxing consumption across the economy [S3].
